title: Higgsfield Platform Mastery
headings: The model roster (what to use when)
text: Higgsfield Platform Mastery The model roster what to use when Higgsfield is model-agnostic — it hosts many engines under one credit pool. Third-party model guides rank them this way tiers: Free / Low 0.1–2 credits / Mid 2–10 / Premium 10+ : Need Model Tier --- --- --- Top-tier cinematic video + native audio Kling 3.0 Premium Epic scale / spectacle Sora 2 Premium Nature / landscapes + reference images Veo 3.1 Premium Artistic / stylized video Wan 2.6 Mid Fast iteration Seedance 2.0 Pro Mid VFX / fluid motion Minimax Hailuo 2.3 Mid Budget-friendly video Kling 2.5 Turbo / Higgsfield DoP Lite Free–Low Image side: Soul 2.0 fashion/aesthetic, free , Soul Cinema cinematic stills with film grain and era-aware styling , Nano Banana Pro photorealistic, low cost , Soul Cast AI actor generation . Key insight: a clip made through Higgsfield on the Kling engine is a Kling clip — what differs is how you buy it shared credit pool and what you can steer presets vs raw prompt control . Going to Kling directly exposes controls Higgsfield's preset UI hides: end-frame pinning, multi-reference elements , multi-prompt shots, 3–15s durations. Cinema Studio — the filmmaking layer Cinema Studio is Higgsfield's director-mode workspace: - Camera movement controls: static, handheld, zoom, pan, dolly, orbit and more — several moves can be stacked in one shot - Genre settings: Action, Epic, Drama, Comedy, Horror — the whole scene follows the genre's look and pacing - Era selection: regrade to look like the 1960s, 1980s, 1990s, or today - AI Cast: build custom AI actors with chosen look, outfit, era, personality - Scene building: place locations and props, shape the frame - Emotions: choose what each character shows - Color grading: fine-tune color, temperature, contrast, presets - Multiple references: upload many reference images to guide generation - Real-time co-directing: invite teammates onto one project - AI assistant: help with camera angles, lighting, prompts, script-to-shot breakdowns It isn't tied to one model — pick the best engine per shot. Generation controls that matter - Start frame: upload or generate the opening image; the clip grows from it. This is the single biggest quality lever. - End frame where supported : pin exactly where a camera move finishes — turns drift into intention. - Camera movement presets: faster than prompt engineering; pick the move, don't describe it. - Duration: longer clips cost more and drift more. Short, locked shots chain better than long wandering ones. - Aspect ratio: match your delivery format from the first generation, never crop later. Turbo vs Standard thinking - Standard / Premium models Kling 3.0 etc. : hero shots — faces, dialogue, key story beats. - Turbo / Lite models: iteration, B-roll, establishers, tests. Draft cheap, render the winners expensive. - One clip at a time, quality-gated: a failed clip never chains. Re-prompt, don't hope. Reliability rules 1. Never spend credits on a guess — pre-check the prompt against the checklists in prompt-engineering.md . 2. Failed/NSFW generations aren't billed on the API path; verify billing behavior in the app before a big batch. 3. Credits reset each billing cycle and don't roll over — plan usage so paid credits don't evaporate. 4. Higgsfield open-sourced three of its own AI films with every prompt, camera setting, and asset published — mine those before inventing your own pipeline. Sources - https://higgsfield.ai/creator-hub/help-center/ai-models/how-do-i-create-and-use-a-soul-id-character - https://www.thehypemagazine.com/2026/10/09/what-is-higgsfield-ai-uses-features-pricing/ - https://www.meltflexai.com/blog/higgsfield-alternatives - https://github.com/ivan-meer/higgsfield-ai-prompt-skill/blob/HEAD/skills/higgsfield-models/SKILL.md - http://dev.to/mckennachapman/higgsfield-api-in-practice-prompt-to-editorial-photo-and-the-defaults-that-bite-f0c

title: Higgsfield Prompt Engineering
headings: The anatomy of a prompt that works
Camera phrasing that the models obey
text: Higgsfield Prompt Engineering The anatomy of a prompt that works Treat the prompt as a directing system, not a description. Every generation should specify, in order: 1. Subject — who/what, locked identity 2. Micro-action — one believable action, not three 3. Environment — where, with subtle motion in it 4. Camera behavior — one intentional move see below 5. Lighting design — explicit and physical "golden-hour side light, long shadows" 6. Visual style — cinematic, anamorphic, film grain, era 7. Emotional tone — the feeling of the shot 8. Physics & motion details — how things move cloth in breeze, steam rising 9. Rendering quality modifiers — 4K, shallow depth of field, stable architecture Missing layers = randomness. "Slow dolly push-in" beats "zoom in." Explicit lighting beats "nice lighting." Camera phrasing that the models obey - Push-in / reveal: "the camera slowly dollies toward the subject with smooth stabilized movement" - Pull-back / scale: "the camera slowly pulls backward, gradually revealing the enormous environment surrounding the subject" - Orbit: "camera orbits 360° around the subject" - Pan: "slow camera pan across the scene" - Stacked moves: Higgsfield's Cinema Studio supports several moves in one shot — but one motivated move beats two unmotivated ones. Rule: every movement needs a purpose. Ask what the move reveals or withholds. The Soul ID prompting rule When a Soul ID character is active, do not re-describe the face or core features — the Soul ID handles that. Describe only what changes: wardrobe, setting, action, expression, camera, light, style. Good: "The Soul ID character now wears a formal black suit, standing at a podium addressing a conference room. Camera: dolly in toward her face. Style: cinematic, cool corporate lighting." The exclusion block Always exclude what breaks cinematic output: morphing faces, extra limbs, melting hands, warping architecture, flicker, watermark-like artifacts, text in frame unless wanted . Put it in every prompt, not just the risky ones. Per-shot discipline - One shot = one fully self-contained prompt. Restate the full premise every time — the model has no memory of your last clip. - Don't ask for too many actions in five seconds. One action per clip. - Keep the frame uncrowded. Fewer subjects = fewer failure modes. - Image-to-video start frame first beats text-to-video for control. Generate the still, approve it, then animate. Common failure modes and fixes Failure Fix --- --- Face morphs mid-shot Shorter clip; Soul ID or reference image; re-generate from a locked start frame Melting hands Keep hands out of frame or still; exclude "deformed hands"; crop in post Camera drift unmotivated Pin an end frame; name one explicit camera move; shorten duration Identity drift across shots Soul ID; same seed discipline; approved-frame library as start frames Flicker / texture boil Regenerate; avoid overly busy backgrounds; stabilize in post Plasticky faces in wide shots Shoot closer; composite a close-shot face in post Sources - https://higgsfield.ai/creator-hub/help-center/ai-models/how-do-i-create-and-use-a-soul-id-character - https://github.com/ianfr13/higgsfield-ai-prompt-skill/blob/HEAD/mnt/user-data/outputs/higgsfield/skills/higgsfield-soul/SKILL.md - https://github.com/servanter/ai-magic/blob/HEAD/content/blog/best-ai-video-generators-2026-sora-runway-kling-pika-comparison.mdx - https://medium.com/@gencaycubuk/i-tested-dozens-of-runway-prompts-this-framework-creates-cinematic-ai-videos-every-time-e171658033e1 - http://answerbeam.blogspot.com/2026/10/how-to-generate-video-from-image-with.html

title: Soul ID Deep Dive
headings: When to use it / when to skip it
text: Soul ID Deep Dive What it is Soul ID is Higgsfield's character-consistency layer: train it once on photos of one person and the same face appears across every generation — any style, pose, lighting, or angle. It's the equivalent of casting the same actor for the entire film. A reference image anchors a single generation but drifts across many. Soul ID trains a reusable identity once and holds it. How to train official requirements From Higgsfield's help center: 1. Open higgsfield.ai → Soul → Train new character 2. Prepare photos: 20 or more of the same person up to 80 supported - High-quality and well-lit - Face from different angles and expressions - No sunglasses, no heavy shadows, no cropped faces - Include at least one full-height photo - Recent photos for the most accurate likeness - Only your own face or someone who gave permission 3. Upload and start training — takes a few minutes 4. Name the character 5. Generate — select it in the Character tab Using it in production - Soul ID locks identity; everything else follows your prompt. Wardrobe, setting, action, camera, light — all prompt-driven. - Prompting rule: never re-describe the face. Describe only what changes from the base character. - Works across the Soul family Soul 2.0, Soul Cinema, Cinema Studio, Marketing Studio, supported video models . - Caveat: Soul IDs are tied to the model they were trained in — a character trained in Soul 2.0 may need retraining for Soul Cinema. Verify before a big shoot. When to use it / when to skip it Use: multi-shot sequences, short films with a recurring protagonist, series content, AI influencers, brand mascots, action sequences needing the same hero. Skip: single one-off shots overkill , or when you want maximum creative variation — consistency limits style range. Identity drift: causes and fixes - Drift across many generations: re-anchor with the trained Soul ID selected; don't fall back to per-generation reference uploads. - Wide-shot face collapse: faces go plasticky at distance — shoot closer, or composite a close-shot face in post. - Feature drift: keep a character sheet front, 3/4, side reference and use it as the reference image when drift appears. - Never fabricate identity frames. The trained Soul ID is the identity authority — every clip's face must trace back to it, never to an invented start frame. Sources - https://higgsfield.ai/creator-hub/help-center/ai-models/how-do-i-create-and-use-a-soul-id-character - https://www.thehypemagazine.com/2026/10/09/what-is-higgsfield-ai-uses-features-pricing/ - https://github.com/ianfr13/higgsfield-ai-prompt-skill/blob/HEAD/mnt/user-data/outputs/higgsfield/skills/higgsfield-soul/SKILL.md - https://github.com/mahshid1378/owner-avatar-higgsfield-ai-prompt-skill/blob/HEAD/skills/higgsfield-soul/SKILL.md

title: The $100K Festival Playbook
headings: The rules that shape your production
What won before: the Action Contest
text: The $100K Festival Playbook The "$100,000 prize" is real — it's the 3rd-place and Audience Choice tier of the Higgsfield Global Film Festival , a $1,000,000 competition. This chapter is the playbook for it. The competition --- --- Total prize pool $1,000,000 across 14 winners 1st place $500,000 2nd place $200,000 3rd place $100,000 Audience Choice $100,000 Honorable Mention ×10 $10,000 each Runtime 3–5 minutes Eligibility Higgsfield subscribers, 18+, solo or teams up to 4, worldwide Jury: Edwin Catmull Pixar co-founder, five-time Oscar winner and Phedon Papamichael two-time Oscar-nominated cinematographer, Ford v Ferrari among others — an Oscar-caliber panel, not a marketing jury. Timeline 2026 edition : submissions opened early August, deadline mid-September 2026; screening and shortlist through early October; jury review early-mid October; winners announced end of October 2026. The rules that shape your production - Minimum viable submission: final video with Higgsfield's watermark and packshot, plus a public post of the same video on Instagram, YouTube, X, or Reddit must stay public, no login wall — a private account disqualifies you . - Music, voice, and sound design must be AI-generated , uploaded into the submission project, with rights held by the creator. - No real person's face or voice — not even your own. - One film gets one prize; one participant/team gets one prize across all entries. Prizes don't stack. - Any genre, any story. Strategy notes - The honorable-mention math: 10 shots at $10,000 is a different bet than one shot at $500,000. Ten finalists get paid — aim for the top fourteen, not just the top spot. - The jury reads like a real film festival. Catmull and Papamichael reward story, cinematography, and craft — not prompt cleverness. Direct for them, not for AI Twitter. - Sound is judged. AI-generated music/voice/sound is mandatory — a silent film or stock-music film is leaving points on the table by rule, not just taste. - Higgsfield open-sourced three of its own AI films with every prompt, camera setting, and asset published. Study those before spending a credit. What won before: the Action Contest Higgsfield's earlier Action Contest 8,752 submissions, 139 countries shows what this jury DNA rewards: - 1st $150,000 : "GRANDMA vs WASP" — Muhannad Nassar & Simon Meyer. Never met in person; async workflow across time zones in Cinema Studio. Action short, decentralized production. - 2nd $100,000 : "CUPID" — Shestak Nikolay, actor/filmmaker. Concepts that would need prohibitive traditional budgets — AI used for scale, not novelty. - 3rd $50,000 : "SCRATCH" — Ash & Aram Gevorkyan, made in five days . Director + 3D/VFX generalist duo; production value so high audiences mistook it for a studio trailer. - 20 honorable mentions at $10,000 each. Pattern: experienced filmmakers using AI for impossible scale, tight teams, real craft — not tech demos. Submission checklist - 3–5 minute final cut, watermark + packshot included - All music/voice/sound AI-generated, files in the submission project, rights cleared - No real faces or voices anywhere in the film - Public social post live Instagram/YouTube/X/Reddit , account public - Submitted before the deadline in your timezone - Team of 4 or fewer, all 18+, active subscription Sources - https://higgsfield.ai/blog/higgsfield-global-film-festival - https://aivideosensei.com/guides/higgsfield-global-film-festival-guide - https://medium.com/@sanwsman7/i-didnt-believe-ai-could-make-a-real-film-until-i-tried-higgsfield-ai-de0b4ee68072 - https://www.linkedin.com/posts/the-ai-journal ai-aifilmmaking-higgsfield-activity-7490768602418253824-Ofvk - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=babNcxpwnx0 Action Contest winner reveal - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZoqzD NMa4w "CUPID" — 2nd place, $100K

title: Story Structure for AI Short Films
headings: Story Structure for AI Short Films
text: Story Structure for AI Short Films The short-film engine A 3–5 minute AI film needs exactly three things: 1. One want — the protagonist wants something concrete, visible on screen 2. One obstacle — something specific stands in the way 3. One turn — the moment everything changes Most AI-film losers are tech demos with no second act: pretty shots, no turn. Judges especially Oscar-caliber ones punish this first. The festival-short template - Cold open 0:00–0:30 : drop into the world mid-action. No setup, no title cards explaining the premise. - Escalation 0:30–2:30 : the want meets the obstacle, pressure builds. Each shot raises the stakes or deepens the world. - Reversal 2:30–3:30 : the turn — the plan fails, the truth lands, the choice gets made. - Button 3:30–5:00 : one final image that reframes everything before it. End on the image, not on explanation. Writing for the model Design scenes around what AI renders well; write away from what it doesn't. Lean into: single subjects, strong silhouettes, weather and atmosphere, landscapes, slow deliberate motion, objects and environments, stylized looks. Write around: complex hand action, crowd choreography, intricate dialogue scenes, fast fight choreography, text/signage in frame, real people or voices festival rules forbid them anyway . The constraint is the style: the best AI films don't hide the medium — they pick stories the medium tells better than live action could impossible scale, dream logic, metamorphosis . Scene design checklist per scene - One clear want visible in the frame - One action per shot, five seconds or less each - The turn is a visual event, not dialogue - Every scene either raises stakes or deepens world — never both vaguely, never neither - The ending image is planned before the first shot is generated

title: Cinematic Language
headings: Shot sizes — what each one is for
Lighting — write it like a gaffer
text: Cinematic Language The shot vocabulary and camera grammar that make AI video read as cinema instead of a screensaver. Shot sizes — what each one is for Shot Use --- --- Extreme wide World, scale, isolation Wide Geography — where the story happens Medium Action and dialogue — the workhorse Close-up Emotion, decision, detail Extreme close-up Texture, eyes, objects that matter Festival rule of thumb: earn your close-ups. Wide → medium → close builds pressure; starting close spends it. Camera movements — the working lexicon Move Prompt phrasing Good for --- --- --- Dolly in / push-in "camera slowly dollies toward the subject, smooth stabilized movement" Portraits, reveals, rising tension Dolly out / pull-back "camera pulls backward, revealing the environment around the subject" Scale, aftermath, loneliness Pan "slow camera pan across the scene" Surveys, transitions between subjects Orbit "camera orbits around the subject" Hero moments, product, dance Crane "camera rises and pulls back, revealing the scene from above" Endings, scope Handheld "subtle handheld shake, documentary feel" Urgency, realism — use sparingly Static "locked-off static camera" Dialogue, tension, confidence "Slow dolly push-in" beats "zoom in" every time — name the physical move, not the effect. Motivated vs unmotivated: every move must reveal or withhold something. A drifting camera with no purpose is the 1 tell of amateur AI video. If you can't say why the camera moves, lock it off. Lighting — write it like a gaffer Vague lighting gets vague images. Specify direction, quality, and color: - Direction: side light, backlight/rim, top light, underlight - Quality: hard noon sun, soft overcast, flickering torchlight, neon spill - Color/temperature: golden-hour warmth, cold blue night, sodium-orange street - Motivation: every light needs a source in the world — window, lamp, neon sign Example: "dramatic golden-hour side lighting with long shadows" will always beat "nice lighting." Composition - Rule of thirds: place the subject off-center; give the frame somewhere to breathe - Depth staging: foreground, midground, background all doing something — this is what makes AI shots feel expensive - Leading lines: roads, corridors, light beams pulling the eye to the subject - Negative space: emptiness is a compositional choice — isolation, scale, dread - Don't overcrowd: fewer subjects per frame = fewer failure modes The "cinematic" recipe "Cinematic" is not a word you add — it's five things combined: 1. Camera — one intentional movement 2. Subject — one believable action 3. Environment — subtle motion dust, smoke, cloth, water 4. Lighting — explicit, motivated, consistent 5. Texture — film grain, anamorphic cues, shallow depth of field Example: "Slow cinematic dolly forward toward an ancient temple entrance. Priests walk calmly up stone steps while torch flames flicker. Thin smoke rises into warm evening air. Cloth banners move gently in the breeze. Stable architecture, realistic human motion, dramatic golden-hour lighting." Note: every movement has a purpose, and the prompt asks for exactly one action per subject. Sources - http://answerbeam.blogspot.com/2026/10/how-to-generate-video-from-image-with.html - https://github.com/servanter/ai-magic/blob/HEAD/content/blog/best-ai-video-generators-2026-sora-runway-kling-pika-comparison.mdx - https://medium.com/@gencaycubuk/i-tested-dozens-of-runway-prompts-this-framework-creates-cinematic-ai-videos-every-time-e171658033e1 - https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z8IaWHEYfpY

title: Character Consistency
text: Character Consistency The technical discipline of keeping people and worlds stable across shots. This is where most festival entries die. The identity stack ranked by reliability 1. Trained identity Soul ID : the gold standard. Train once on 20–80 photos; the face holds across every generation. See higgsfield/soul-id-deep-dive.md . 2. Character sheet as reference: front / 3/4 / side views of the character, used as the reference image whenever drift appears. 3. Per-generation reference upload: anchors one generation; drifts across many. Fine for single shots, not films. 4. Text description alone: weakest. Never rely on prose to hold a face across 50 shots. Wardrobe and props lock - Write the wardrobe once, in exact language, and paste it verbatim into every prompt: "worn brown leather jacket, white t-shirt, dark jeans, scuffed boots." - Props get the same treatment: one description, reused exactly. - If the wardrobe changes mid-film it should, for story , that's a new locked description — never improvise it per shot. World consistency - Locations: generate and approve a master still of each location first. Every shot in that location starts from it or references it. - Lighting continuity: lock time of day and light direction per scene. "Golden-hour side light from frame left" in every prompt of the scene. - Era/grade: pick the era and color palette up front Higgsfield's era selection helps ; don't grade shot-by-shot and hope. The chaining discipline - Last-frame chaining: every clip starts from the last frame of the previous approved clip. Never fabricate a start frame. - Approved-frame library: keep every approved still/frame. New shots start from library frames, not fresh generations. - Rejection rules: a clip fails if the face drifts, wardrobe changes, the light flips, or the camera moves without motivation. Failed clips don't chain — they get re-prompted. - One human per start frame for character-led work : crowded frames multiply failure modes. The consistency checklist before any generation - Identity system chosen and trained Soul ID for films - Wardrobe description locked, verbatim - Location master stills approved - Light direction + time of day locked per scene - Start frame is real approved frame or trained identity , never invented

title: Directing Performance in AI Video
text: Directing Performance in AI Video AI models don't act. They render plausible arrangements of pixels that read as acting when the direction is specific enough — and collapse into mannequin theater when it isn't. This chapter is the directing discipline behind believable AI performance, drawn from productions that solved it in public. The core problem Passport Rush's team documented it openly: AI struggles with subtle character acting. The failure has a shape: - Faces average toward neutral — micro-expressions collapse into a pleasant blank - Emotion labels "she looks devastated" produce stock expressions, not felt ones - Dead, glassy eyes — the single fastest tell of an undirected AI performance - The Verge's review of Cully Hill Boys noted "occasionally weak character interactions" as a visible limit even at $2M The fix is not a better model. It's direction written the way actors need it — as tasks , not adjectives. Direct, don't describe ONEIRIC's acting skill tig-acting-task replaced emotion labels with acting tasks entirely. The closing rule of that production: direct, don't describe — scene event, motive, goal, obstacle, tactic. Instead of description Write direction --- --- She looks devastated She is trying not to cry in front of him — jaw set, eyes on the door He is furious He is deciding whether to hit him — weight shifting forward, hands opening and closing They are in love She keeps finding reasons to stand closer; he keeps noticing and not moving away He is nervous He is rehearsing what to say — lips moving silently, thumb rubbing the ring Every entry on the right is a playable tactic — something a body can do. Models can't render "devastated." They can render a jaw set and eyes fixed on a door. Give the eyes a job The single highest-leverage performance note in the research: "dead, glassy eyes are never fixed with lighting — they're fixed by giving the eyes a job." The CINEDANCE prompt architecture gives GAZE/EYELINES its own block before blocking. In practice: - Name the eyeline target per beat: Mara holds on Vex's hands until "the ledger" — then snaps to his eyes - Eyes move between targets; they never "look sad into the middle distance" - Avert, hold, search, track — eye verbs are direction, not decoration - In dialogue coverage, the listener's eyes do half the acting — cut to the listener If a performance feels dead, check the eyes first. Nine times out of ten there's no eyeline written. One feeling per shot AI can't play an arc inside a single clip. It can hold one tactic for 4–8 seconds. So: - Break emotional turns into separate shots — the turn happens in the cut - The reaction shot is your best friend: AI renders listening better than it renders complex feeling - Moment-to-moment tactics tied to dialogue words the tig-acting-task block form : each line gets its own tactic, each tactic its own shot if needed The director's read Before generating a scene, ONEIRIC's pipeline produced a "director's read": the one shared event every character lives through, plus each character's physical channel for it. Everyone in the scene is experiencing the same event — but grief lives in Mara's hands, in Vex's jaw, in the kid's feet. Write the event once, then assign each character their channel. This is what keeps ensemble scenes from becoming four mannequins emoting at the camera. Casting the face Consistent identity reads as good acting. A face that drifts 5% between shots reads as a bad performance even when the "acting" is fine: - Lock the face anchor; never re-run the base portrait - State changes dirt, wounds, tears are masked integrations, not re-generations - For recurring characters, identity systems Soul ID and equivalents beat per-prompt description The audience forgives a limited performance from a consistent face. It never forgives a great "take" from a stranger. Ration the close-up Micro-acting is the weakest link in every current model. Spend close-ups at emotional peaks — that's where the audience looks ha

title: Color Grading AI Footage
text: Color Grading AI Footage Every AI generation arrives with its own built-in grade — the model's idea of what "cinematic" looks like, baked into the pixels. On a multi-shot production, that's 40 different colorists who never met. The colorist's job on AI footage is unification : bringing neighboring shots to one look. The two places color lives In the plate before generation . Lens character, palette direction, texture, time-of-day — baked into the location/character image plates. What you bake, you don't have to fix. The ONEIRIC rule: the plate itself becomes the lens. In the grade after generation . Shot-to-shot matching, the show look, technical delivery. What the plate couldn't hold. Decide per element which place it lives. Anything the video model keeps dropping belongs in the plate. Anything that needs to move across the whole film belongs in the grade. The unification pass Before any creative grading, unify. Pick one hero shot per scene as the reference. For every other shot: 1. Match exposure and white balance to the reference scopes, not eyes 2. Match contrast curve — AI generations vary wildly in black level 3. Match saturation — see the de-plasticize stack below 4. Only then apply the creative look Do the unification pass over the location set before generating where possible the ADILIADA production did this — it's cheaper than discovering mismatch in the grade. The de-plasticize stack AI footage has a recognizable syndrome: over-smooth gradients, over-saturated color, waxy skin, a sheen over everything. The fix, in order: 1. Desaturate 10–20%. AI oversaturates by default. This one move does half the work. 2. Add fine film grain. 35mm grain breaks up the smooth gradients that scream synthetic. Grain is the fastest anti-plastic pass in existence. 3. Subtle chromatic aberration at high-contrast edges. Real lenses have flaws; perfect edges read as rendered. 4. Soften, don't sharpen. Plastic + sharp = worse. A whisper of diffusion beats any sharpening pass. 5. Skin last. Skin is the hardest surface — if it's waxy, a dedicated skin-refinement pass or slight diffusion on skin tones only. Check the whole stack on a big screen. Defects invisible on a laptop appear at 4K. Matching across models Different models have different "house grades" — Kling's contrast curve isn't Veo's. When a scene mixes models: - Unify harder: match to the reference before any creative look - The plate matters more: shared plates across models do more than any grade can - If two models won't match, re-generate the outlier rather than torturing the grade The show look Once unified, the creative grade. For AI film, restraint wins: - One look for the film, with scene-level variations — not a new look per scene - Work in passes: primary whole image → secondaries skin, sky, key objects → texture grain, halation, gate weave if period - Halation and bloom flatter AI highlights, which tend to clip harshly - Decide the grain philosophy early: one grain for the film, applied at the end, over everything — it's the final unifier Scopes, not eyes Grade with waveforms and vectorscopes. AI footage lies to eyes — the "cinematic" built-in grade is designed to flatter on first glance. Check: - Blacks actually reach black AI loves milky shadows - Skin tones sit on the skin-tone line vectorscope - Saturation doesn't clip in any channel Delivery - Festival masters: 16:9 or 21:9 composed not cropped for the ratio, up to 4K - Broadcast-safe levels; -1 dBTP audio ceiling is the sound department's job, but don't crush the picture to compensate - Keep the pre-grade masters. When the festival asks for a revision, you re-grade — you don't re-generate. The grading checklist - Look decided per element: plate vs grade - Unification pass before creative grading reference still per scene - De-plasticize stack applied: desat, grain, CA, soften - Skin checked on a big screen - Multi-model scenes matched or re-generated - One show look, scene variations — not a look per scene - Scopes

title: Sound, Music & Audio
headings: Sound design (the layer that sells reality)
text: Sound, Music & Audio Sound is half the picture. Amateur AI films are silent; winners are designed. Festival rules require AI-generated music, voice, and sound — this isn't optional. Native audio Some video models generate audio natively with the clip. Rules: - Keep it when it's ambient texture: room tone, wind, rain, crowd murmur, footsteps. - Strip it when it's dialogue, music, or anything prominent — regenerate those deliberately. - Never let native audio be your only sound layer. It's a bed, not a mix. Sound design the layer that sells reality Every scene needs three layers: 1. Bed: ambient tone of the location room, street, forest, wind — runs under everything. 2. Foley: footsteps, cloth, object handling — the sounds that make movement feel physical. 3. Accents: designed hits for story beats — the turn, the reveal, the button. AI SFX tools can generate all three from text prompts. Describe sounds the way you describe shots: specifically and physically. Score - AI music generators take prompts like: "ambient synth, 85 BPM, rising tension, no vocals." - Temp-track discipline: cut to a temp score first, then generate the final score to the locked cut — never score to a moving target. - No vocals unless the story needs them; score serves the story, never shows off. - The festival requires AI-generated music with rights you hold — keep the generation receipts. Dialogue - When AI dialogue works: short lines, clean delivery, minimal background noise in the reference audio. - When it doesn't: long speeches, overlapping voices, emotional extremes. Write around these — visual storytelling over talk. - Lip-sync pipeline: generate the visual first, then sync: feed clean WAV audio into the platform's lip-sync Pika and Runway both offer it; clean audio in = believable sync out . - Rule: if the line doesn't change the story, cut it. Festival shorts win on images. The audio checklist - Ambient bed under every scene - Foley on all physical movement - Score generated to the locked cut - Dialogue minimal, clean, synced - Final mix: dialogue score bed nothing fights the story - All audio AI-generated with rights documented festival requirement

title: Editing Pipeline
text: Editing Pipeline From selects to festival-ready export. Assembly - Selects discipline: generate 2–4 takes per shot, keep the best one. Kill darlings — a beautiful shot that doesn't serve the story is a deleted shot. - Cut to the story, not the footage: the shot list is a plan, not a prison. If a generated shot is better than planned, re-cut around it. - Keep ratios honest: 45–75 shots for a 3–5 minute film. Fewer, better shots beat more, weaker ones. Transitions and pacing - Cuts over effects. Hard cuts are invisible; dissolves and wipes announce themselves. Use transitions only when time or place changes. - Pacing math: action sequences cut faster 1–2s shots , emotional beats breathe 4–6s . Vary rhythm deliberately — monotony is the enemy. - The J-cut/L-cut: let audio lead or lag the picture cut. Instant professionalism, costs nothing. Color - Match AI shots to each other first: different models and prompts produce different grades. Normalize before styling. - One LUT direction for the whole film: pick the palette in pre-production era selection helps and apply consistently. - The "expensive" grade: restrained contrast, skin tones natural, shadows with detail. Over-saturated teal-and-orange reads cheap. - Free tools: CapCut handles LUTs, grain, contrast, and saturation well enough for festival delivery. VFX touch-up - Cleanup passes: inpaint glitches, stabilize micro-jitter, remove stray artifacts. - Face composite: plasticky wide-shot faces get replaced with crops from close-shot frames. - Grain: a light film-grain overlay unifies shots from different models — the cheapest consistency tool in post. - Upscale last: finish the edit, then upscale the final timeline — never upscale individual clips and re-edit. Delivery - Export specs: match the festival's required format, resolution, and codec exactly. - Watermark + packshot: the Higgsfield festival requires both in the final video — build them into the export, not as an afterthought. - Watch it on three screens: phone, laptop, TV. If it only looks good on one, the grade isn't done. - The 24-hour rule: lock the cut, sleep, watch fresh. Every flaw you catch now is one the jury won't. The delivery checklist - Picture lock before color and mix - Color matched across all shots, one palette - Sound mix final dialogue score bed - VFX cleanup pass complete - Watermark + packshot embedded - Exported to festival spec - Watched fresh on multiple screens

title: The Long-Form Pipeline: Making AI Films at 20+ Minutes
headings: The Long-Form Pipeline: Making AI Films at 20+ Minutes
The Cully Hill Boys — 110 min, ~$2M, 4 weeks, 28 people
ONEIRIC — 20 min, made for the $1M festival
Passport Rush — hybrid, 18 scenes in 3 days
Dreams of Violets — 75 min, Tribeca official selection
Team roles for a small AI feature crew
What to steal — the long-form checklist
text: The Long-Form Pipeline: Making AI Films at 20+ Minutes Short films are won with great prompts. Long films are won with systems . Everything in this chapter comes from productions that actually shipped long-form AI work — most of it open-sourced by Higgsfield — and every number carries its source. Where the research couldn't verify something, it's flagged. The core insight Across every documented long-form AI production, the through-line is the same: assets before shots, always. Locked character sheets, locations, and props exist as named, versioned records before any video is generated. The working shape is: - brief.md — logline, tools, pre/prod/post plan - script.md — the screenplay - registry.md — the constants: named looks per world, one verbatim descriptor per @-tagged asset - one shotlist.md per scene — each shot: number, seconds, one-line goal, the entire prompt verbatim , look: , optional source: - log.md — version history per shot: version, what changed, takes, verdict Cully Hill Boys published a 137-entry version log . ONEIRIC generated 41,118 assets for ~20 minutes . The scale of waste — not the cost per clip — is the real budget line. Case snapshots The Cully Hill Boys — 110 min, ~$2M, 4 weeks, 28 people The first fully AI-generated feature with licensed celebrity likenesses Israel Adesanya, Quinton "Rampage" Jackson, streamer N3on, Matt "MK" Kiatipis . Seedance 2.5 for video + speech, Claude for prompt crafting, Seedream and Nano Banana for polish. ~1,000 production-ready assets across ~100 locations in 4K. About half the budget ~$1M went to compute; the rest covered likeness licensing, creative direction, screenplay, and finishing. Forty percent of the crew had no prior AI experience — the roles were directorial and editorial, not ML. Key mechanics: - Character sheets built from the licensed talents' photos and audio, locking face, body, clothing, and voice before generation began. Talent supplied ~2 minutes of voice audio; biometrics were contractually purged within 30 days. - A shared canvas system held sheets, locations, props, and state so parallel teams stayed in continuity. - Average prompt: over 3,000 words with 10+ image references per scene per Higgsfield co-founder Alex Mashrabov . - Open-sourced: prompts, production logs, workflow docs, character cards, raw assets — via Higgsfield Academy and YouTube. ONEIRIC — 20 min, made for the $1M festival Correction: earlier versions of this guide described a Cannes premiere for ONEIRIC. The research found no source connecting it to Cannes — its official description says it was made on Cinema Studio 4 for the $1M Higgsfield Global Film Festival . The Cannes-adjacent AI screening was Hell Grind's , and that was a third-party industry showcase, not an official selection. Four friends, four genres Troy battle, galactic cruiser chase, griffin flight, dorm-room drama . Open-sourced: every Seedance asset and prompt, plus Claude skills for scripting tig-scene-engine , acting direction tig-acting-task , and shot prompting tig-diagram . Key mechanics: - The blocking diagram: when a shot needs precise multi-character staging, words stop working. A color-coded schematic outline is attached last among references so photos win the style vote; the prompt binds each color to a character tag. Rules: front view from the camera's side never a top-down plan — "video models think in frames, not blueprints" , letters live in prompt text only, edits address colors not characters "move the BLUE figure" . - The consistent-lens-look trick: asking for an anamorphic look in the video prompt fails — optics drift shot to shot. Fix: bake the optics into the location image plate. The plate itself becomes the lens. - Two-pass character sheets: Soul Cinema makes the face in close-up the identity anchor ; Soul 2.0 builds full-body looks from it. Hard rule: the base portrait is never re-run through any model — variants are integrated with masks around the base pixels. Re-running a portrait is how

text: AI Video Platform Field Guide Every major platform, honestly assessed. Strengths, weaknesses, costs, and what each is actually best at. The field Platform Signature strength Weakness Cost signal Best for --- --- --- --- --- Higgsfield All-in-one: many engines, Soul ID, Cinema Studio presets, camera moves Preset UI hides raw controls; shared credit pool obscures per-model price Basic 120 / Pro 600 / Max 1,800 credits/mo; tiers Free–Premium 10+ credits Filmmaking workflow, character-led series Kling direct Photoreal physics water, fire, smoke ; end-frame pinning; multi-reference elements Prompt engineering required, no hand-holding ~0.6 units/sec 720p standard ~$0.084/sec ; 0.8 pro; 3.0 native 4K Hero shots when you want raw control Runway Gen-3/Gen-4 Reference-image start + Motion Brush for exact motion control; human-centric scenes Weaker without a strong start image Paid tiers, full commercial rights Ads, human scenes, precise motion Sora Epic scale, spectacle, narrative interpretation prompts as mini-screenplays Access/cost; less steerable moment-to-moment Premium tier Vast scenes, ambitious concepts Luma Dream Machine Cinematic experimentation, smooth motion Consistency weaker than leaders Varies Dreamlike / experimental passages Pika Lip-sync, character animation, playful effects; most permissive creatively Less "cinematic" out of the box Subscription Dialogue, social, stylized work Hailuo / MiniMax VFX and fluid motion Prompt nuance Mid tier Action, fluid dynamics Veo Nature/landscapes, reference-image fidelity, long coherent passages Premium cost Premium tier Landscapes, documentary feel Wan Artistic / stylized video Less photoreal Mid tier Stylized sequences Seedance Fast iteration speed Top-end polish trails Kling/Sora Mid tier Drafting, volume work Platform-specific prompting notes - Sora: write prompts like mini-screenplays — scene direction, character actions, environment in sequential order. - Runway: start with a strong reference image, then Motion Brush for movement. More predictable than text-only. - Kling: keep prompts concise and direct; elaborate prose underperforms. Use motion templates. - Pika: stack creative effects; for lip-sync feed clean audio with minimal background noise. Ownership and rights verify before commercial use - Sora: users own generations Opt-out of training data use on Enterprise . - Runway: full commercial rights on paid tiers. - Kling: commercial rights on Pro and above. - Pika: full ownership on paid tiers; free tier restricts commercial use. The honest take No single platform wins every shot. Festival-grade films are hybrid: pick the engine per shot, match color in post, and nobody will know. See when-to-use-what.md . title: When to Use What
text: When to Use What The decision tree for picking the right tool per shot. Festival-grade films are hybrid — nobody will know if you match color in post. Decision rules Shot need Reach for Why --- --- --- Character close-up / dialogue Higgsfield + Soul ID Kling 3.0 engine Identity lock + top-tier faces + native audio Epic scale / impossible environments Sora 2 Best vast-scene coherence Nature / landscapes Veo 3.1 Reference-image fidelity, natural texture Precise motion control Runway + Motion Brush Paint exactly where movement happens Fast action / fluid VFX Hailuo 2.3 Fluid dynamics strength Stylized / artistic passages Wan 2.6 Style over photorealism Lip-sync dialogue Pika Clean-audio-in, synced lips out Drafting / volume / tests Seedance 2.0 Pro or Kling 2.5 Turbo Speed and cost Budget hero on a budget Kling direct end-frame pinning, elements Raw control without preset markup The hybrid pipeline 1. Plan per shot, not per film. The shot list gets a model assignment column. 2. Anchor on one identity system Soul ID so faces survive platform-hopping. 3. Generate in passes: all drafts on cheap/fast models → approve → heroes on premium. 4. Normalize in post: one color pipeline, one grain overlay, one audio mix. This is what makes mixed sources invisible. 5. Never switch models mid-scene unless you have to — consistency is cheaper than correction. Cost-aware ordering - Rough out the whole film on Turbo/Lite first cheap . - Identify the 10–15 hero shots that carry the story. - Spend premium credits only on heroes and dialogue. - Everything else ships from the draft pass with a good grade. Anti-patterns - Using one platform for everything out of loyalty — you pay in quality somewhere. - Premium-rendering a shot before the edit is locked — re-edits waste the expensive generation. - Mixing aspect ratios across shots — pick delivery format on day one.

title: Credit Math
headings: The no-guess pipeline (credit-saving order of operations)
Per-clip costs across platforms (third-party estimates, Oct 2026 — re-verify before budgeting)
Rules of thumb from working filmmakers
text: Credit Math Professional quality without burning the budget. The standing rule: never spend credits on a guess. What things cost Higgsfield Plan Credits/mo Rough video yield --- --- --- Basic 120 ~15 standard clips Pro 600 ~75 standard clips Max 1,800 ~225 standard clips Model tiers: Free Soul 2.0, DoP Lite · Low 0.1–2 credits · Mid 2–10 · Premium 10+ . A standard Kling clip runs ~8 credits; premium/longer/Cinema Studio sessions cost more. Going direct to Kling: ~$0.084/sec at 720p standard, ~$0.112/sec pro, ~$0.42/sec native 4K. Credits reset each billing cycle and don't roll over — schedule production so paid credits don't evaporate. The no-guess pipeline credit-saving order of operations 1. Write the shot list first. Every clip planned before a single credit is spent. 2. Draft cheap. Turbo/Lite models for composition and motion tests. 3. Render heroes expensive. Premium models only for faces, dialogue, and key story beats. 4. One clip at a time, quality-gated. A failed clip never chains — re-prompt, don't hope. 5. Price before you send. Estimate cost per request before batching; verify balance before a batch, not after. Where to spend vs save - Spend: hero close-ups, dialogue shots, the trailer moment, the final shot. - Save: establishers, B-roll, transitions, montages — Turbo is fine. - Free tools that don't look free: CapCut for color/LUTs/grain, stabilization in post instead of re-rendering, compositing fixes face swaps from close shots instead of regenerating wide shots. The festival budget frame A 3–5 minute festival film at ~4 seconds per shot is 45–75 shots. At draft-then-hero discipline, most shots need 2–4 generations to land. Budget for 150–300 generations and plan the credit pool before starting — or split across platforms by shot type. Per-clip costs across platforms third-party estimates, Oct 2026 — re-verify before budgeting Platform Est. cost per clip Notes --- --- --- Vidu ~$0.05 Cheapest; free tier non-commercial PixVerse ~$0.07 Budget pick Pika ~$0.17–0.61 Standard plan has NO commercial use — trap Hailuo MiniMax ~$0.44–0.76 Best price/quality ratio per multiple sources Luma ~$0.30–1.20 Kling 3.0 ~$0.40 Strong motion/camera control Veo 3.1 Fast ~$0.40–0.50 Native audio; cheapest premium-quality route Runway Gen-4.5 ~$1.44–1.50 Fastest generation Higgsfield Seedance 2.5 ~$2.48 Aggregates many models Sora 2 ~$0.40–2.00 Longest clips up to 25s Rules of thumb from working filmmakers - ~$80 per finished minute of film, all-in. - 3–5 takes per keeper; 2–5x raw-to-finished multiplier. Budget the rejects, not the hero renders. - $40–165 in credits for a disciplined 3-minute short; $150–300+ without discipline. - Resolution ladder: 480p drafts → 720/1080p heroes → upscale to 4K in post native 4K ≈ $1/sec . - Audio-first: lock voiceover/soundtrack before generating video — cheap audio prevents expensive timing-mismatch re-rolls. - Cautionary: one documented Higgsfield pilot burned ~$260,000 in credits over 4 days for ~8 usable shots — brute-force iteration without craft. The no-guess rule exists because of math like this. Try it Run your numbers in the interactive budget calculator ../budget.html — runtime, shot length, model, and discipline in, cost envelope out. text: Festival Winner Breakdowns Shot-by-shot lessons from films that actually won money. Every entry below was found with an attributed source — nothing invented. Items the research could not verify are flagged. The pattern before the films Across Runway AIFF, Project Odyssey, Reply AIFF, the Higgsfield Action Contest, and MIT's hackathon, judges reward the same things: story over spectacle, authorial intent, character/POV discipline, originality, sound design, and polish as the floor. They punish: visible morphing/inconsistency, generic "AI slop," tech demos without narrative, and AI that pulls focus from the story. Distilled: narrative cohesion + committed POV + intentional AI use + pro-grade sound + consistent visuals. Originality is the tiebreaker; polish is the entry ticket. The case studies "Total Pixel Space" — Jacob Adler, Runway AIFF 2025 Grand Prix 9:28 essay film. A voiceover calculates how many possible images could exist in digital space; surreal tableaux illustrate it. Inspired by Borges' "The Library of Babel." Tools: image generators + synthetic voices + Runway Gen-3; over a year in production, tens of thousands of images. Field: ~6,000 submissions; judges included Harmony Korine and Gaspar Noé. Why it won: concept-first, AI-thematic — the medium is the message. The critic's take: it treats AI's glitches and eeriness as material to think with, carried by old-fashioned style and narrative. Steal: make the film about what the medium does, or make the medium invisible — never halfway. "Get Me Out" — Daniel Antebi, Runway AIFF 2024 Grand Prix 6 min. Aka flees a shadowy suburban house that stores his haunting memories, embodied by a blood-red figure of pure muscle. About displacement and mental health. Tools: Luma 3D environment capture , Runway video-to-video, ComfyUI rotoscoped a performer, re-skinned him as muscle . Why it won: hybrid craft — live-action emotional performance with invisible, motivated AI VFX. Antebi's own read: the artist-jurors resonated with the storytelling, not the tool cleverness. Steal: shoot the emotion for real; use AI only for what the budget couldn't do otherwise. "A Face Only a Mother Could Love" — Robert Gaudette, Runway AIFF 2026 Grand Prix + Reply AIFF 2026 winner Photorealistic short: Marcel, a solitary Parisian dancer born with facial disfigurement; a woman's approach sparks connection. Tools: Grok, Nano Banana, Seedance — chosen, in his words, as the only viable way to film the screenplay without budget, cast, or crew. It started as an old screenplay experiment, never meant for festivals. Why it won: intimacy and POV — tight shots establishing point of view in a way reviewers don't associate with AI imagery; nothing read as slop. Steal: a real screenplay beats a prompt. Character-first photorealism is now a proven winning lane. "GRANDMA vs WASP" — Muhannad Nassar & Simon Meyer, Higgsfield Action Contest 1st, $150,000 Action short. The duo never met in person — async remote workflow across time zones in Higgsfield's Cinema Studio. Field: 8,752 submissions, 139 countries. Judges Jason Zada, Buralqy, Jama Jurabaev prioritized storytelling and directorial intent over technical polish. Why it won: proof that decentralized AI production works — two strangers, one film, no studio. Steal: team up across disciplines; the contest rewards directorial intent, not solo prompt heroics. "CUPID" — Nikolay Shestak, Higgsfield Action Contest 2nd, $100,000 Tagline: "Aggression has become the norm. It's time for silence." Shestak is an established actor/filmmaker using Higgsfield for concepts that would need prohibitive traditional budgets — and planned to fund an indie superhero film with the prize. Why it won: the archetype judges love — a professional using AI for impossible scale, not novelty. Steal: bring a filmmaker's eye; the tool is the budget, not the idea. Build your entry like a winner — assembly order
text: Entry Craft Teardowns: How the Winning Films Were Actually Made The companion chapter lists who won and why . This one is the how — the production techniques behind festival-winning entries, broken into steps you can copy. Every teardown follows the same shape: the technique , the craft principle , copy it actionable steps , and the budget/time footprint where it's documented. 1. The async remote workflow — "GRANDMA vs WASP" $150K, Higgsfield Action Contest The technique. Directors Muhannad Nassar and Simon Meyer never met in person. They built the film async across time zones inside Higgsfield's Cinema Studio — one shared project where generations, prompts, and assets were all visible to both collaborators. No studio, no set, no shoot days; the "set" was a shared generation window. The craft principle. Judges Jason Zada, Buralqy, Jama Jurabaev said they prioritized storytelling and directorial intent over technical polish — in a field of 8,752 submissions from 139 countries. The remote workflow won because the directing was centralized even though the labor was distributed: one vision, two executors, zero drift between them. Copy it. - Write a one-page director's intent doc before generating anything: logline, tone references, the single emotion each act must land. - Work in a shared project, not DMs — every prompt, generation, and select lives where your collaborator can see and fork it. - Split by discipline, not by scene: one person owns performance/character, the other owns camera/action. Review each other's selects daily. - Lock a style bible on day one one style line, aspect ratio, grain/grade, lens language so two people can't drift apart. Footprint. Two people, zero travel, consumer AI subscriptions. The budget went to time, not gear. 2. The five-day sprint — "SCRATCH" $50K, Higgsfield Action Contest The technique. Director/musician Ash Gevorkyan + 3D/VFX generalist Aram Gevorkyan made a trailer-grade action short in five days. Audiences mistook it for a studio-backed theatrical trailer. The weapon was trailer form: sound, cutting, and pacing doing the heavy lifting while the imagery stayed in short, high-energy bursts that never linger long enough to break. The craft principle. Fluency beats time. Five days of fluent execution beats five weeks of hesitant prompting — because the duo already knew their tools cold, every generation was a deliberate choice, not an experiment. Copy it. - Cut a trailer, not a short: 60–90 seconds, three acts hook / escalation / title card , music-driven pacing. - Keep shots short 2–4 seconds . Short shots hide consistency breaks; long takes expose them. - Build the sound design first or in parallel — trailer percussion, risers, and hard-hitting SFX sell "studio" more than any pixel does. - Budget generations per shot: 3–5 variations for hero shots, 1–2 for connective tissue. Decide selects fast. Footprint. Five days, two specialists, deep tool fluency. The most replicable winning formula in this chapter. 3. The hybrid pipeline — "Passport Rush" and "Get Me Out" The technique. "Passport Rush" combined hand-drawn storyboards + Blender previz + AI animation, publishing every prompt and asset. "Get Me Out" Runway AIFF 2024 Grand Prix captured a real 3D environment in Luma, shot a real performer, then used Runway video-to-video and ComfyUI to rotoscope and re-skin him as a blood-red muscle figure. The craft principle. Shoot the emotion for real; use AI only for what the budget couldn't do otherwise. Both films put a human performance or human draftsmanship at the center and used AI as the impossible layer — never the entire layer. Jurors working artists, in Antebi's case resonated with the storytelling, not the tool cleverness. Copy it. - Board on paper or in Blender first. If the story doesn't work as boards, it won't work as generations. - Capture or shoot anything with a human body in it for real — even a phone previz gives the AI motion something truthful to hold onto. - Use video-to-vide
